paras: In January 1903 white residents of Mississippi warned postal officials to stop employing Black mail carriers, serving notice on the postmaster at Jackson and threatening a post-office inspector in Lincoln County with tar and feathers. No violence was reported, but the dispatch was printed in papers from Washington to Minnesota and Texas as evidence of a spreading "crusade against negro Federal officeholders."

The reports placed the warnings within a broader campaign in Mississippi against Black men holding federal positions. The Lincoln County threat referred back to Indianola, warning the inspector against siding with a Black employee "like he did at Indianola." The same dispatch noted that the New Orleans States had warned President Roosevelt that appointing Black men to federal offices in the South would "lead to blood-shed."

According to a special sent from Jackson through New Orleans, white people served notice on the Jackson postmaster that Black carriers on the star mail routes must be discontinued "at once." The papers named neither the senders nor the carriers, and did not give the date of the notice.

On about January 9 or 10 a similar warning reached post-office authorities in Lincoln County, where postal officials had employed a Black man to deliver mail on a rural route. White residents told the inspector that the carrier would not be permitted to perform the service and that, if the inspector took the carrier's side, he would be "treated to a dose of tar and feathers."
The coverage does not report any reply from the postmaster, the inspector or the Post Office Department, nor whether the carriers kept their routes.

The story ran as a single dispatch, datelined New Orleans on January 9 in the St. Louis Republic and the Saint Paul Globe and January 10 in the Alexandria Gazette and the Washington Times. Headlines framed it as a "Crusade Against Negroes" or against "Negro Officeholders," while the Washington Times led with the threat itself: "Postal Inspector May Wear Tar and Feathers." Smaller papers carried it the following week, including the Iron County Register in Missouri, the Sharp County Record in Arkansas under the slur-headline "Do Not Want Cuffy," and the Bryan Morning Eagle in Texas, which credited the Galveston News.

In Mississippi the Tupelo Journal printed the special under the headline "Do Not Want Negroes to Fill Office" and added its own comment. The paper wrote that Roosevelt had stirred up trouble by siding with Black officeholders and that he was "shootin' too high" in trying to "mortify and humble the white people of this state." No coverage of the Jackson or Lincoln County warnings was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Warnings against Black mail carriers in Jackson and Lincoln County, Mississippi
bases: The reports describe a notice and a threat of tar and feathers aimed at ending the employment of Black mail carriers, with no act of violence reported (A1, A2).
Every report traces to one special from Jackson sent through New Orleans, reprinted with small changes (A1, A2, A6); no independent local or Black-press account was found.

accounts.label: Special from Jackson via New Orleans
accounts.gist: White people served notice on the Jackson postmaster to discontinue Black star-route carriers, and in Lincoln County warned the inspector that a Black rural carrier would not be allowed to serve and that the inspector faced tar and feathers if he took the carrier's side.

accounts.label: Tupelo Journal comment
accounts.gist: Reprinted the special and said Roosevelt had stirred up trouble by siding with Black officeholders and would fail to humble the white people of Mississippi.

framing.detail: Northern and border papers ran the special under headlines such as 'Crusade Against Negroes' and 'Crusade Against Negro Officeholders' without comment.
The Washington Times headlined the threat itself: 'Postal Inspector May Wear Tar and Feathers.'
The Tupelo Journal headed it 'Do Not Want Negroes to Fill Office' and added that Roosevelt was 'shootin' too high' in trying to humble the state's white people.
The Sharp County Record headed the reprint with the slur 'Do Not Want Cuffy.'

conflicts.note: Variants of a single dispatch; the earliest printings (Jan. 10 papers) carry Jan. 9 or Jan. 10, so the Lincoln County warning fell on about Jan. 9-10. The Jan. 12 dateline is a later reprint's.
